questions.text: Evaluate the contour integral of 1/(z^2 + 1) around |z| = 2 using residues.

solution.steps: Poles at $z=\pm i$, both inside $|z|=2$. Write $\dfrac{1}{z^2+1}=\dfrac{1}{(z-i)(z+i)}$. By Cauchy's Integral Formula applied at each pole: residue at $z=i$ is $\dfrac{1}{2i}$, at $z=-i$ is $\dfrac{1}{-2i}$. Sum of residues $=0$, so the integral is $2\pi i\cdot0=0$.
solution.commonMistakes: Only accounting for one of the two poles inside the contour.

questions.text: Why must the Cauchy–Riemann equations hold at a point for a function to be complex differentiable there, and why is that not sufficient on its own?
Every analytic function is infinitely differentiable — explain why this has no real-variable analogue.
Write the Cauchy–Riemann equations in polar form and prove them: du/dr = (1/r) dv/d(theta), dv/dr = -(1/r) du/d(theta).
questions.originalText: Write the Cauchy–Riemann equations; prove their polar form: ∂u/∂r = (1/r)∂v/∂θ, ∂v/∂r = −(1/r)∂u/∂θ.

solution.hint: Use the chain rule to convert x=r cos(theta), y=r sin(theta) into the Cartesian Cauchy-Riemann equations.
solution.steps: With $x=r\cos\theta,\,y=r\sin\theta$: by the chain rule, $u_r = u_x\cos\theta+u_y\sin\theta$ and $u_\theta = -u_xr\sin\theta+u_yr\cos\theta$, and similarly for $v$. Substituting the Cartesian C–R equations $u_x=v_y,\,u_y=-v_x$: $v_\theta = -v_xr\sin\theta+v_yr\cos\theta = u_yr\sin\theta+u_xr\cos\theta = r(u_x\cos\theta+u_y\sin\theta)=ru_r$. This gives $u_r=\dfrac1r v_\theta$. A parallel substitution gives $v_r=-\dfrac1ru_\theta$.
solution.finalAnswer: u_r = (1/r) v_theta and v_r = -(1/r) u_theta, derived directly from the Cartesian Cauchy-Riemann equations via the chain rule.
solution.examReady: Substitute x=r cosθ, y=r sinθ into the Cartesian C–R equations using the chain rule for u_r, u_θ, v_r, v_θ, then algebraically isolate the polar form.
solution.commonMistakes: Sign errors when applying the chain rule to ∂/∂θ, since it introduces an extra factor of r and a sign flip from differentiating cosθ/sinθ.
